study.title: 1 Kings 12 - The division of the kingdom and the corruption of the cult
study.overview: This chapter shows the rupture between Rehoboam and the northern tribes, caused by the arrogant response of the new king to the demands of the people for relief. The text at the same time presents the sovereignty of God leading events and human responsibility for foolish and oppressive choices. After the political division, Jeroboam strengthens his new kingdom with measures that also deform worship: he creates alternative centers, images of worship, non-Levital priests and a feast invented by himself. Thus, the chapter links power, politics and worship, showing that the infidelity to the Lord erodes both government and religion.

outline.title: Rehobone receives the request of the people and chooses the wrong advice
outline.explanation: Israel meets in Shechem to confirm Rehoboam as king. Jeroboam returns from Egypt and leads the demand for relief from the burdens imposed by Solomon. Rehoboam asks for three days, first consults the elders and then the young people of his court, and rejects the path of humility. The harsh response reveals contempt for the people and prepares the crisis.

outline.title: Rejection of Rehoboam provokes the revolt of the tribes
outline.explanation: On the third day, the king reaffirms his threat rather than serving. The text states that this happened according to the ordination of the LORD, to fulfill the word already given through Ahijah. Israel breaks with the house of David, stones Adoram, and makes Jeroboam king over the northern tribes, and Rehoboam left only Judah and Benjamin.

outline.title: The word of the LORD prevents war, but Jeroboam corrupts the worship
outline.explanation: Rehoboam gathers an army to try to recover the kingdom, but Shemaiah transmits the divine command so that he does not war against his brothers. Then Jeroboam seeks to consolidate his power with religious strategies: it reconstructs cities, creates two golden calves, institutes high places, chooses priests outside the Levitical lineage and invents a feast in the eighth month. The chapter culminates in his sacrifice at Bethel, marking a cult shaped by fear and convenience, not by fidelity to God.

study.context: The chapter describes the immediate transition after the reign of Solomon. The meeting in Shechem shows that the unity of the kingdom was still in dispute and that the northern tribes had political and religious weight. The text also recalls the Lord's previous word on the division of the kingdom, showing that the conflict was no surprise to God, although it emerged from real and guilty human decisions.
study.theology: The narrative teaches that leadership without service produces rupture. Rehoboam fails because he rejects the wisdom of the elders and uses authority to crush, not to shepherd. At the same time, the chapter states that God rules even on political crises to fulfill his word, without annulling the guilt of human agents. Then Jeroboam exemplifies a pragmatic religious policy: it adapts the cult to preserve power, but this becomes sin. The text condemns the creation of a proper religion, made to control the people and to avoid their fidelity to the Lord in Jerusalem. It is also clear that leadership sin has collective effects: a superb decision divides the kingdom, and an invented cult drags Israel into ruin.

scholarViews.insight: The commentary highlights that Shechem was an important strategic and religious location for the northern tribes, so that Rehoboam needed their support to rule a united kingdom.
The comment points out that the division of the kingdom shows how the glory of Israel, so high in Solomon's reign, began to decline rapidly in the next reign.

The comment suggests that the expression about the LORD in 12:15 should be read carefully: the revolution came from God in his providence, but the immediate cause also includes Rehoboam's folly, cruelty, and tyranny.

questions: In what situations have I heard advice that reinforce my pride rather than call me to humble service?
What forms of leadership, at home, in the church or at work, can become oppressive when I just want to preserve control?
What practices or decisions can I be inventing from my heart in the name of convenience, but that weaken my faithfulness to God?
study.practice: Examine your leadership decisions in the light of this chapter: listen to wise advice, answer meekly and seek the good of people before defending their own position. Reject also any attempt to adapt worship or obedience to God for convenience, fear, or calculus. If you influence others, use this influence to serve, not to intimidate. And when conflicts arise, remember that not every strategy that preserves power preserves the truth.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided are in English and are partial in some points; therefore, the study is limited to what was explicitly said in them and in the biblical text presented. No external data other than that appears in the chapter and the excerpts provided were not used. The numbering of verses was followed from the first to the last, according to the text provided.
